newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Dreams become reality for Belgrade leaders.
newsitem.headline: Dreams become reality for Belgrade leaders.

text.p: Serbia's opposition coalition, which won a three-month battle with ruling socialists for control of Belgrade's city council, took control of the capital on Friday and pledged to work hard to transform it.

Newly-elected mayor Zoran Djindjic was optimistic that the coalition-led council would meet the expectations of Belgraders, despite inheriting a city desperate for reforms and modernisation and very little money to pay for it.

Djindjic was the only candidate for mayor and was elected with 68 votes to loud applause in the chamber. Ending the socialists' 50-year grip on power in the city, he took over the chair of the assembly session within minutes of the vote.

But the first council session had hardly got underway when members of the Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) and the Radical Party walked out of the chamber, disagreeing on agenda items and the refusal to discuss abolition of a city tax.
Even among the three party members of the Zajedno (Together) coalition differences of style soon emerged.
One of the three co-leaders, bearded novelist Vuk Draskovic, said he was opposed to any kind of celebration despite a rally planned for later to celebrate the coalition's election victories.
"This is the beginning of hard, hard, very hard work and not the beginning of celebrations. I am completely against celebrations, against singing," he told Reuters in English.
"Until today we were in opposition. We had a right to dream, to make all kinds of promises. From today we're facing reality and we will be responsible for the life in this city."

But Djindjic believes hope counts for more than hard cash. "With good management and good organisation we can complete a lot of business with far less money than is thought to be needed," he told Reuters.

"People are satisfied with little, people in Belgrade do not have such big expectations, they will be happy if things on which their everyday life depends function better than they have done so far, which I believe will be achieved."
He said he wanted the city government to make its finances public and would demand the Serbian government gives Belgrade "the authority which will enable it to solve its problems".

Zajedno forced Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's socialists to recognise its gains in local elections held in November with daily street protests, which involved half a million people at their height.
They attracted worldwide media attention and support from foreign governments which turned to reproach when Milosevic unleashed his security police on the demonstrators.
Zajedno halted the protests when the socialists recognised election victories but leaders say two goals remain to be met.
They want Milosevic's authoritarian government to free the country's heavily-controlled media and create fair conditions for parliamentary and presidential elections later this year.
The coalition now has the majority in Belgrade with 69 seats out of 110 on the council, though socialists still control both the Serbian and Yugoslav governments.
After the walk-out Zajedno councillors voted to remove the management of Studio B, a Belgrade radio and television station run by the city. Djindjic said he wants it to be independent.
Later on Friday the coalition was due to remove a five-pointed star, representing communism, from the Belgrade parliament building and a rally was planned for 8.30 p.m..
